title: Histology of the lymph node

blocks.title: Orientation and learning map
blocks.description: Begin with the whole organ, then move from the capsule toward the medulla and finally trace lymph through the node.

blocks.text: A lymph node is a bean-shaped, encapsulated organ positioned along lymphatic vessels. Its cells and supporting stroma are arranged into cortex and medulla; the cortex is further divided into outer cortex and inner cortex, also called the paracortical region.

blocks.title: After this lecture, you should be able to
items: Locate lymph nodes and describe their overall shape and capsule
Identify capsule, trabeculae, cortex, paracortex, medulla, and hilum
Distinguish primary and secondary lymphoid nodules
Relate germinal-center zones to B-cell selection and maturation
Recognize the T-cell-rich paracortex and high endothelial venules
Compare medullary cords with medullary sinuses
Trace lymph from afferent lymphatics to the efferent lymphatic vessel

blocks.title: Whole-organ orientation
blocks.alt: Diagram dividing a lymph node into cortex, paracortex, and medulla
blocks.caption: Use the compartment map to orient every later microscopic feature from the capsule toward the hilum.

blocks.heading: Where lymph nodes are found
blocks.text: Lymph nodes are distributed throughout the body along the course of lymphatic vessels. They are found in the axilla and groin, along the great vessels of the neck, and in large numbers in the thorax and abdomen, especially in the mesenteries.

blocks.heading: Capsule and trabeculae
blocks.text: The node is surrounded by a dense connective-tissue capsule composed of collagen and elastin fibers with interspersed fibroblasts. Trabecular extensions project from the capsule into deeper regions of the node. As trabeculae penetrate the node, they continue into reticulum fibrils composed of type III collagen, adding structural support.

blocks.label: Surface polarity
blocks.text: The convex surface is pierced by numerous afferent lymphatic vessels that conduct lymph into the node. The opposite concave region is the hilum, where the efferent lymphatic vessel exits.

blocks.title: Cells named in the lecture
rows: The most common cells; B cells dominate follicles and T cells dominate the paracortex

blocks.title: Recognizing the organ on a section

blocks.text: A cross section shows three histologic regions: a superficial cortex, a deeper paracortex, and a central medulla. The capsule encloses the node; trabeculae extend inward; the cortex contains primary and secondary nodules; the paracortical region lies deep to the superficial cortex; and medullary cords and sinuses converge toward the hilum.

blocks.prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the major regions from the outside toward the center of a lymph node?
options: Medulla, paracortex, outer cortex
Outer cortex, paracortex, medulla
Paracortex, medulla, outer cortex
Outer cortex, medulla, paracortex
blocks.answer: The superficial outer cortex is followed by the deeper paracortex and then the central medulla.

blocks.title: Outer cortex: sinuses and lymphoid nodules

blocks.text: The outermost lymphoid layer is the outer cortex. It contains the subcapsular sinus, cortical sinuses, and lymphoid nodules.

blocks.heading: Subcapsular and cortical sinuses
blocks.text: The subcapsular sinus is the first space entered by lymph arriving through afferent vessels. It contains a loose network of reticular cells and fibers. Lymph then enters cortical sinuses, which are branches of the subcapsular sinus. Because these channels travel along the trabecular network, they are also called intermediate or trabecular sinuses. They share the same basic structure as the subcapsular sinus.

blocks.title: Primary versus secondary lymphoid nodules
rows: B lymphocytes undergoing activation, selection, and maturation

blocks.title: Germinal center: zones and B-cell fate

blocks.text: Lymphatic nodules, with or without germinal centers, are formed mainly by B lymphocytes embedded within the irregular population of cortical cells. A germinal center can be subdivided into dark, light, and mantle zones. Each zone supports a different part of B-cell affinity maturation.

blocks.title: Three zones of a germinal center
rows: Produces B-cell variants with mutated antibodies; supplies cells to the light zone
Centrocytes, follicular dendritic cells, helper T cells, and macrophages
Affinity-based selection: strong binders persist, weak binders undergo apoptosis
Quiescent B cells with small cytoplasmic volume and heterochromatic nuclei; follicular dendritic cells; occasional helper T cells and macrophages
Peripheral ring surrounding the germinal center

blocks.title: Secondary lymphoid nodule
blocks.alt: Microscopic view of a lymphoid nodule with a pale germinal center and surrounding mantle
blocks.caption: Use the contrast between the germinal center and its surrounding lymphocytes to recognize a secondary nodule.

blocks.heading: Selection in the light zone
blocks.text: Centrocytes interact with follicular dendritic cells that display intact antigen on their surface. Centrocytes with high-affinity binding persist, while weak binders undergo apoptosis. Resident macrophages remove apoptotic B cells, and helper T cells support the remaining B cells and foster cellular maturity.

blocks.heading: Possible B-cell outcomes
blocks.text: B cells may remain in the lymph node and mature into antibody-secreting plasma cells, mature into memory B cells, or re-enter the systemic circulation.

blocks.prompt: Where are highly mitotic centroblasts found?
options: Mantle zone
Light zone
Dark zone
Medullary sinus
blocks.answer: Centroblasts are concentrated in the dark zone and provide source cells for the light zone.

blocks.prompt: What determines whether a centrocyte persists in the germinal-center light zone?
options: Strong binding to antigen displayed by follicular dendritic cells
Direct contact with a medullary sinus
Entry through an afferent lymphatic vessel
Loss of all interaction with helper T cells
blocks.answer: Centrocytes with high-affinity binding persist; weak binders undergo apoptosis.

blocks.text: The paracortex lies deep to the outer cortex. Its margins blend with the superficial cortex and the deep medulla. Its principal distinguishing features are the absence of lymphoid nodules and the large number of T lymphocytes in its stroma.

blocks.label: High endothelial venules
blocks.text: The paracortex contains specialized high endothelial venules, or HEVs, lined by cuboidal endothelium. Most lymphocytes that enter the lymph node from the blood do so through these channels. Similar specialized venules are present in mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue throughout the gastrointestinal tract, but they reach their highest level of development in lymph nodes.

blocks.prompt: Which combination best identifies the paracortex?
options: B-cell nodules and a subcapsular sinus
T lymphocytes, no nodules, and high endothelial venules
Plasma-cell cords and medullary sinuses
Dense connective tissue and afferent lymphatics
blocks.answer: The paracortex is a T-cell-rich, nodule-free region containing high endothelial venules.

blocks.title: Medulla: cords, sinuses, and final filtration

blocks.text: The medulla is the deepest layer of the lymph node. It is divided functionally and histologically into medullary cords and medullary sinuses.

blocks.title: Medullary cords versus medullary sinuses
rows: Cord-like projections extending centrally from the paracortex
Distended channels interlacing between the cords
Plasma cells, B cells, and T cells
Discontinuous endothelium with a network of reticular-cell processes on the luminal surface
Final point of filtration for circulating lymph
Terminal continuation of cortical sinuses; converges at the hilum to form the efferent lymphatic vessel

blocks.text: Lymphatic vessels are lined by a single layer of squamous endothelium. Valves promote unidirectional flow from afferent lymphatic vessels into the lymph node and then out through the efferent lymphatic vessel.

blocks.title: Route of lymph through one lymph node
blocks.pathway: Lymph transit through the lymph node
blocks.description: Follow the location of lymph from entry at the convex surface to exit at the hilum.

steps.title: Afferent lymphatic vessels
steps.description: Numerous afferent vessels pierce the convex surface and bring lymph into the node.

steps.title: Subcapsular sinus
steps.description: This is the first intranodal space entered by lymph. This subcapsular space surrounds the node except at the hilum and contains a loose reticular network.

steps.title: Cortical or trabecular sinuses
steps.description: Branches of the subcapsular sinus carry lymph along the trabecular network.

steps.title: Medullary sinuses
steps.description: Terminal continuations of cortical sinuses provide the final filtration point through discontinuous endothelium and reticular-cell processes.

steps.title: Efferent lymphatic vessel
steps.description: Medullary sinuses converge at the hilum and lymph leaves the node through the efferent vessel.

blocks.title: Source wording clarified
blocks.text: The final sentence of the source slide says that lymph leaves through afferent vessels. The same slide describes one-way flow from afferent to efferent vessels, and the lecture diagram shows efferent exit at the hilum. The sequence above therefore uses efferent vessel for the exit step.

blocks.prompt: What is the correct route of lymph through the node?
options: Efferent vessel, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinus, medullary sinus
Afferent vessel, medullary sinus, cortical sinus, subcapsular sinus
Afferent vessel, subcapsular sinus, cortical sinus, medullary sinus, efferent vessel
High endothelial venule, cortical sinus, afferent vessel, hilum
blocks.answer: Lymph enters through afferent vessels, passes through subcapsular, cortical or trabecular, and medullary sinuses, then exits through an efferent vessel at the hilum.
